# Predicting High Income from Census Attributes {.unnumbered}

*A developer log on tabular ML, fairness, and interpretability*

This book is a **narrative rewrite** of my end-to-end machine learning study on the [UCI Adult (Census Income)](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/datasets/adult) dataset. I built a reproducible pipeline, compared classical and neural models, evaluated a final LightGBM classifier on a held-out test set, and then asked the harder questions: what features drive predictions, and do error rates differ across demographic subgroups?

The [original academic report](https://github.com/jt-09/uci-adult-data-ml/blob/main/reports/report.md) and [PDF](assets/main.pdf) ([release copy](https://github.com/jt-09/uci-adult-data-ml/releases/download/v1.0/main.pdf)) are **unchanged**. This site reuses the same exported figures and tables - no pipeline rerun required to read it.

## Results at a glance

| Item | Value |
|------|-------|
| Selected model | LightGBM (tuned on train CV) |
| CV macro F1 (train only) | 0.815 |
| Test macro F1 | 0.818 |
| Test ROC-AUC | 0.930 |
| Test Brier score | 0.087 |
| Positive class rate | 23.9% (imbalanced) |

## Reproducing the underlying work

Source code, configs, and pipeline scripts live in the [GitHub repository](https://github.com/jt-09/uci-adult-data-ml). If you want to regenerate artifacts from scratch, start with the README quick-start - this book only **points at** the exported results.

**Rule I followed throughout:** never tune or select models on the held-out test set. Selection uses 5-fold CV macro F1 on the training split only.

Let's start with why I picked this dataset and what the raw census rows looked like after cleaning.
